For this reason, it may sometimes seem that Phenomenology is speaking about reality from beginning to end.
But what appears there is not reality itself. It is only reality as reflected in “false” knowledge—that is, reality as the content of this knowledge.
Of course, even false knowledge is real in the sense that it actually occurs within reality. It therefore reveals reality in some way.
And we will see that such knowledge is “false” only because it presents itself as universal or complete while in fact remaining one-sided.
If we examine false knowledge, we can isolate the aspect of reality that it does reveal. If we then combine all these aspects, we obtain full or true knowledge of reality.
But carrying out that analysis of the reality revealed through cognition is simply not the task of Phenomenology itself.
Thus, although Phenomenology studies only knowledge, it does not separate the “form” of knowledge from its “content.” It studies knowledge of reality.
And the reality embraced by Phenomenology in the fullest sense is concrete reality.
What exists concretely is not “reality in general,” but the real material world: the natural world of mountains, rivers, and forests, as well as the technical world of houses, roads, and cars.
And this real world genuinely includes the real subject who knows it, together with that subject’s historical, social, and political world.
So when Phenomenology studies knowledge of concrete reality, it studies knowledge of both the natural and the human world.
Let us say it once more: it studies knowledge of this real world, not the world itself in its reality.
But knowledge of this world is itself real, and Phenomenology studies not only knowledge of concrete reality but also the concrete reality of knowledge.
Real, concrete knowledge exists in the real world in the person of human beings.
Phenomenology therefore studies not “consciousness in general” or some kind of “world-reason,” but human consciousness and human reason.

In other words, it studies concrete human knowledge of the concrete world. It studies not the world in its reality, but the world as it is revealed or manifested to human beings—that is, if we like, the appearance of the world to humanity, its phenomenon.
This is where the name comes from: phenomeno-logy, a discourse or science of appearance and appearances.
Now, the real world includes humanity itself.
So when the world “manifests” itself to human beings, the world is in one sense appearing to itself.
Phenomenology therefore studies not only the ways in which the world appears to human beings, but also the ways in which human beings appear to themselves.
It studies not reality itself but knowledge of reality. And this concrete knowledge is itself nothing other than a human being.
So the “appearance” of the world reveals not so much the world as the human being to whom that world appears.
In this sense, Phenomenology can be described not as a discourse or science of the world—not as a cosmo-logy—but as a discourse or science of human beings: an anthropology.
Yet it studies human beings not simply in their reality, but insofar as they manifest themselves within the world—insofar as they are a “phenomenon.”
The object of Phenomenology is therefore not simply the human being, but the appearance of the human being to the human being.
So although we can call Phenomenology an anthropology, we must now add that it is a phenomenological anthropology.

Since for human beings the appearance of humanity to itself amounts to an experience of oneself—to becoming aware of oneself or becoming self-conscious—we can define Phenomenology still more precisely as the science of human self-consciousness.
And because self-consciousness reveals to human beings a human being within the world, Phenomenology studies not only the appearances of humanity to itself, but also appearances of the world.
It is therefore phenomenology in the full sense of the word.
And because the experience of oneself involves both cognition and knowledge, Phenomenology, in studying self-consciousness, studies both and is therefore also a gnoseology.

At the same time, because it does not separate form from content, and because the content of self-consciousness is knowledge of humanity, it is also—while remaining a gnoseology—a phenomenological anthropology.
So we can call it, with equal justification, a phenomenological gnoseology, a phenomenological anthropology, an anthropological gnoseology, or a gnoseological anthropology.
But Phenomenology does not study human cognition and “appearances” simply out of curiosity. Its specific purpose is to make true knowledge possible.
Self-consciousness interests it only insofar as self-consciousness contains this knowledge, or the real possibility from which Phenomenology itself can arise.
And we know that the only criterion of the truth of knowledge is technical and revolutionary verification.
But revolutionary verification takes place in time. It marks the transition from one form of knowledge, consciousness, and self-consciousness to another.
Phenomenology therefore studies the appearance of human beings to themselves not only at some particular moment, but throughout its temporal—that is, historical—development.
In other words, it studies the becoming, evolution, development, or history of the way human beings—and the world—appear to human beings.
That means the becoming, development, or history of self-experience, and therefore of consciousness, cognition, and knowledge in general.
For this reason, Phenomenology can also be defined as a historical gnoseology or a historical anthropology.
But whatever name we give to Phenomenology—that is, to the book placed before the reader—we must always remember that it is first and foremost precisely a phenomeno-logy: a doctrine of “appearances.”
As such, it differs fundamentally both from gnoseology in the usual sense and from ordinary anthropology.

It differs from ordinary, “Kantian” gnoseology because it does not study some abstraction existing no one knows where—a consciousness and cognition supposedly existing in themselves. It studies a concrete consciousness: the consciousness of a human being.
For this reason, it would actually be more accurate to call the present work a phenomenological anthropology, because those words identify its object and the character of its theme quite precisely.
The object of Phenomenology is the human being; its theme is the phenomenological investigation of the human being.

But if this definition is to become fully intelligible—and if we are to avoid misunderstandings while reading the text—we must explain more precisely how the phenomenological study of human beings differs from the ordinary “scientific” study of them.
The word anthropo-logy, meaning the “science of humanity,” is highly ambiguous and has been used to mean many different things.
Most often, I imagine, it refers to the science that studies human races, both historical and non-historical, and more generally the characteristics of the human body.
Phenomenological anthropology has absolutely nothing to do with this science.
It is interested in knowledge and therefore, ultimately, in speech. It examines human beings only insofar as this is necessary for understanding what they say.

And since we presuppose that only human beings—not animals—can speak coherently, that is, can reveal reality through the meaningful content of discourse, we may say that Phenomenology is interested in human beings only insofar as they are different from animals.
Since there is nothing specifically human in the human body itself, Phenomenology excludes the body from its investigation, together with everything immediately connected with it.
If we want to compare Phenomenology with a general “science” of human beings, therefore, we should compare it not with human anatomy or physiology, but with psychology.
The Greek word psycho-logy means a discourse or science of the “soul” (psychē).
One of the fundamental tasks of Phenomenology is certainly to show that there is no “soul” in the human being.

But if by “soul” we simply mean the aspect of real human existence that distinguishes specifically human existence from merely animal existence, then we could also call Phenomenology a kind of psycho-logy—or, more exactly, that general part of psychology concerned with specifically human “psychic” phenomena.

Still, it is better not to use the word, because—as we will see—Phenomenology has nothing in common with what is ordinarily called psychology, even when psychology understands that the “soul” is not an independent reality or “substance,” but only an aspect of the real human being that can in practice be distinguished from our animal and bodily existence.
Finally, the word “anthropology” is also used for the scientific study of the life of “primitive” peoples: their forms of culture, the basic elements of their worldview, and so on.
Phenomenological anthropology resembles “anthropology” in this sense more closely than it resembles any of the others.

It is true that Phenomenology does not restrict itself to the study of “primitive” humanity. But there is nothing in this concept of anthropology that logically requires us to apply it only to “savages.”

In this sense, “anthropo-logy” is really nothing more than a history of “primitive” peoples in the broadest sense: not merely their political and military—that is, social—history, but also their economic, technical, religious, aesthetic history, and so on.

Because the historical life of “primitive” peoples is relatively simple, we usually study it as a whole. The history of civilized peoples, by contrast, is normally divided into a number of supposedly “independent” histories.
In principle, however, everyone recognizes that dividing a single real process in this way is artificial and undesirable.

These separate “histories” nevertheless form a single whole. So there can be no principled separation between the study of properly historical periods and the study of “prehistoric,” “non-historical,” or “primitive” periods.

If the history of humanity as a whole, embracing every historical and therefore specifically human phenomenon, is called “anthropology,” then Phenomenology most closely resembles anthropology in this sense.
In other words, Phenomenology could be called the complete history of humanity as a whole.

But it is better not to use this name, because Phenomenology differs just as much from what is ordinarily called “scientific” history as it does from what is ordinarily called “scientific” psychology.
Phenomenology is therefore very close in its object to what we ordinarily call history and psychology, while differing sharply from both in the way it treats its theme.

And since anyone who looks for ordinary psychology or ordinary history in Phenomenology is likely to misunderstand it, we need to complete our definition of its object and theme by comparing it with history and psychology and setting it against them.
In one sense, we can say that psychology and history differ from Phenomenology precisely because they present themselves as separate and supposedly independent “sciences.”
Psychology studies what a human being is at a particular moment rather than what human beings were and will become.
More exactly, it tacitly assumes that human “psychic” qualities are eternal and unchanging, and can therefore be studied independently of time—and therefore of history.
Whether it intends to or not, psychology thus recognizes precisely the existence of a “soul”: some thing or “substance” possessing fixed and unchanging qualities or characteristics—“attributes.”
It therefore posits something that remains “eternally” identical to itself in its qualities, much as, say, an oxygen atom, granite, a pine tree, or a tiger does.
A more cautious psychology may avoid making such claims or assumptions. It may say only that it studies those “psychic” qualities that are independent of time and history.
Phenomenology has no objection to this.
It too recognizes that human beings possess certain “eternal” qualities, and it fully accepts that these can be studied—and may well be worth studying—from a scientific psychological point of view.
But Phenomenology holds that these qualities are not specifically human, and therefore do not belong to the theme of its investigation of human beings.
At first sight, then, it seems very easy in principle to draw a boundary between the respective objects of Psychology and Phenomenology.
In practice, of course, there will inevitably be arguments about which qualities are genuinely unchanging and which depend on historical development.
But what matters here is that the objects can, in principle, be distinguished. Possible mistakes in drawing the boundary are not our concern.
Still, this distinction is not enough.

It is true that Phenomenology does not study the unchanging qualities of human beings. But psychology cannot possibly avoid studying, alongside unchanging qualities, some qualities that do change with history and therefore also belong to Phenomenology.
Even when psychology knows that such qualities are “historical,” however, it will still study them independently of history and time.
Psychology takes, so to speak, a cross-section through the historical development of humanity at some particular historical moment, whether present or past.

Phenomenology can then point out that this psychology is not studying the consciousness of humanity “in general,” but, say, the consciousness of the liberal-bourgeois age, or “pagan” or “ancient” consciousness, and so on.
But even if psychology admits this, it does not thereby become Phenomenology.
A phenomenological study of “pagan” consciousness will still differ from a psychological study of the same consciousness.
The difference lies precisely in the fact that psychology abstracts from time, whereas Phenomenology must include time in its investigation.
Psychology is not interested in the origin or genesis of the psychological qualities it studies. Phenomenology describes them as the result of a historical process.
